tldr: To enable humanoid robots to dexterously perform contact-rich tasks like pushing heavy carts and wiping surfaces, the authors propose FLoRe. It is an end-to-end framework integrating force-annotated demonstration collection, a force-predicting policy, and a whole-body controller that balances force tracking with compliance. In real-robot experiments, it achieved an 80% success rate, significantly outperforming a position-only baseline at 26.7%.

(C) A diffusion policy predicts motions and per-hand target forces from vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches. (A) An RL-based hybrid compliance whole-body controller accurately executes these commands while maintaining balance.
overview:
Humanoid robots working in human environments must perform everyday tasks like pushing carts, carrying heavy boxes, and wiping tables. These tasks require precise control over contact forces—how much force to apply to the environment—rather than just kinematic trajectories of limbs. However, conventional imitation learning focuses heavily on position and orientation tracking. This creates problems because actual contact forces vary dramatically with contact stiffness and surface friction. Furthermore, unlike fixed-base manipulators, humanoids are not anchored to the ground. If they exert large forces with their hands without coordinating whole-body balance, they easily topple over.

To address this challenge, the authors developed FLoRe, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. The framework consists of three key components. First, a lightweight, robot-free data collection system where a human operates handheld devices to record whole-body motions and 6-axis contact wrenches simultaneously. Second, a force-reactive diffusion policy that takes images and current forces as inputs to directly predict future hand motions and commanded forces. Third, a reinforcement learning-based whole-body controller that tracks commanded forces accurately while remaining compliant to unexpected external forces.

Across experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot (Unitree G1), the system tackled three challenging contact-rich tasks: pushing a heavy wheeled gantry with a suspended robot, rotating a box with bilateral pinching, and wiping a whiteboard. FLoRe achieved an overwhelming 80% success rate compared to only 26.7% for a conventional position-tracking policy, demonstrating the crucial importance of both observing contact forces and issuing them as explicit control commands.
contributions: Built a scalable robot-free data collection system that simultaneously records body motions and per-hand 6-axis wrenches using handheld force-sensing grippers and wearable trackers.

Developed an RL-based whole-body controller that converts integrated force errors into target position shifts, achieving accurate force tracking under unknown contact stiffness while remaining compliant along unconstrained axes.
Proposed a force-reactive diffusion policy that takes vision, proprioception, and measured forces as inputs to jointly generate whole-body keypoint trajectories and per-hand target force commands.
Demonstrated on a real Unitree G1 robot across three contact-rich tasks that incorporating both force commands and force observations dramatically boosts the success rate from 26.7% to 80%.

sections.heading: Why Position Tracking Fails: Humanoids Need Force Modulation
sections.summary: Everyday humanoid tasks require contact force control, but conventional imitation learning remains biased toward kinematic trajectory tracking. This paper presents FLoRe, a framework handling forces consistently from demonstration collection and policy learning down to low-level whole-body control.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to be useful in human living spaces, contact-rich interactions like pushing carts, shifting heavy loads, and wiping tables are essential. Yet, most prior learning-based loco-manipulation research has focused strictly on generating and tracking kinematic reference trajectories.

This approach has a major pitfall. No matter how accurately a robot reproduces an expert's hand trajectory, small variations in contact stiffness, friction, or object geometry lead to drastically different contact forces. Moreover, unlike fixed-base arms, exerting hand forces causes a humanoid to lose its balance. The robot must coordinate both hands, torso, and legs to maintain stability while simultaneously regulating hand forces.

Solving this problem presents two steep barriers:
- Data barrier: Imitation learning requires large amounts of demonstrations, but existing handheld collection methods only capture motions without contact forces.
- Execution control barrier: Learned humanoid whole-body controllers are typically trained for rigid trajectory tracking or treat external forces merely as disturbances to reject, making sustained, controlled pushing extremely difficult.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors propose FLoRe. From force-annotated human demonstrations collected via handheld devices, a diffusion policy predicts both motions and per-hand target forces. An RL-trained compliant whole-body controller then executes these commands while keeping balance. On the real Unitree G1 robot, FLoRe achieved an 80% success rate versus 26.7% for a position-only approach, proving the decisive value of force modulation.

sections.heading: From Data Collection to Whole-Body Control: Key Differences from Prior Work
sections.summary: This section reviews handheld imitation learning and force control literature to highlight FLoRe's novelty. FLoRe advances beyond prior work by directly measuring 6-axis wrenches, predicting force commands from a policy, and integrating a force-tracking controller that maintains whole-body balance.
sections.details:
### II-A Loco-Manipulation Data Collection and Policy Learning with Force Sensing
Robot-free demonstration collection where humans hold tools has advanced rapidly, popularized by methods like UMI. While some derivatives add force sensors, they rely on fixed-base single-arm manipulators and analytical admittance control. Prior extensions to humanoids only captured whole-body motions without contact forces. Recent humanoid force-sensing setups (such as WT-UMI) only measured 1-axis normal forces at the palm and depended on robot teleoperation data. In contrast, FLoRe requires zero robot-side data during demonstration, recording full 6-axis wrenches and whole-body motions simultaneously.

At the high-level policy tier, prior systems like UniFP applied end-effector force control to quadruped manipulators, but only handled base forces for humanoids. FLoRe predicts per-hand 6-axis wrench trajectories and feeds them directly to the humanoid whole-body controller.

### II-B Force Handling in Low-Level Control
Learned controllers for legged and humanoid robots have traditionally focused either on high stiffness to resist disturbances or low stiffness for passive compliance. Active force tracking—deliberately pushing with a commanded force—remained largely unexplored. Although attempted on quadruped manipulators, those setups relied on inaccurate contact forces estimated from joint torques. FLoRe integrates measured wrist force errors, enabling hybrid compliance: accurate force tracking along commanded directions alongside yielding compliance along uncommanded axes, all handled concurrently with balance control in a single learned policy.

sections.heading: How FLoRe Works: Force Demonstrations, Diffusion Policy, and Hybrid Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: FLoRe consists of three pillars: a whole-body controller that handles unknown stiffness via force error integration (III-A), a force-annotated robot-free demonstration system using handheld grippers and trackers (III-B), and a diffusion policy with force inputs and outputs (III-C).
sections.details:
### III-A Hybrid Compliance Whole-Body Controller with Force Tracking
The low-level controller is a single RL policy maintaining whole-body balance while tracking hand force commands. Because the policy outputs target joint positions, the central challenge is converting force commands into kinematic targets.

The authors introduce an integrated reference generator. Given the hand kinematic reference position $\mathbf{p}^{*}_{h}$ and commanded force $\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{cmd}}_{h}$, it computes a modified target position $\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{h}$ as follows:
$$\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{tgt}}_{h} = \mathbf{p}^{*}_{h} + \frac{\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{cmd}}_{h} + \mathbf{I}_{h}}{K}$$
Here, $K$ is a baseline stiffness (200 N/m) and $\mathbf{I}_{h}$ is the integrated force error. In contact, the target position shifts inside the object surface, pushing the hand forward. However, if the environment stiffness is unknown, a fixed shift yields unpredictable forces. By integrating the error between the measured reaction force $\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{meas}}_{h}$ and the commanded force, the target position automatically adjusts until the contact force matches the command.

A key advantage of this formulation is that it functions seamlessly along uncommanded axes. Suppose a push is commanded along the X-axis while the Z-axis command is zero ($f^{\mathrm{cmd}}_{z}=0$). If an external disturbance pushes the hand along Z, the accumulated integral shifts the target position along the push direction, yielding to the force. Without explicit mode switching, the robot naturally achieves hybrid compliance: tracking commanded forces along active axes while remaining compliant along passive axes.

During simulation training, virtual contact planes with randomized stiffness were placed near the hands. The policy was trained with trapezoidal force pulses while receiving composite rewards for balance maintenance, kinematic tracking, and force tracking.

### III-B Robot-Free Data Collection with Force Annotations
Human demonstrations are collected using two UMI-style handheld grippers alongside HTC VIVE trackers worn on the chest and both ankles. Each gripper features a 6-axis force/torque sensor and a RealSense D405 camera at the wrist. Because identical gripper-and-sensor assemblies are mounted on the real robot, the sensor frames and tool center points (TCP) match between demonstration collection and robot deployment.

### III-C Force-Reactive High-Level Policy Learning
A diffusion policy serves as the high-level planner. It receives observations including wrist camera images, low-dimensional states of relative hand and body poses, and histories of measured hand wrenches. Crucially, forces are used not only as inputs (observations) but also as outputs (target forces per hand). Force inputs provide immediate contact awareness invisible to cameras, while force outputs serve as direct feedforward commands to the low-level whole-body controller.

captions.F2: Operating principle of the hybrid compliance controller. Along the force direction, the target position shifts into the surface via the commanded force and integrated force error, maintaining the desired contact force. Along the compliance direction (no force command), external disturbances shift the target position away via the integral term, yielding smoothly to external forces.
captions.F3: The robot-free force-annotated demonstration interface. The operator holds dual force-sensing, camera-equipped grippers and wears chest and ankle trackers. An identical gripper and sensor setup is mounted directly on the real robot.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Validation on Unitree G1: Pushing, Rotating, and Wiping
sections.summary: FLoRe was evaluated on force tracking accuracy in simulation and across three whole-body contact tasks on a real Unitree G1. Equipped with force commands and observations, the proposed method achieved an 80% success rate, substantially outperforming the position-only baseline at 26.7%.
sections.details:
### IV-A Implementation Details
The low-level controller was trained in Isaac Lab and evaluated in MuJoCo and on the real Unitree G1. Parameters were set to stiffness $K=200$ N/m, integral gain $K_I=0.5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and maximum integral clamp 40 N. The maximum force command was 25 N. The high-level diffusion policy operates at 30 Hz, and the low-level controller runs at 50 Hz.

### IV-B Hybrid Whole-Body Controller Simulation and Real-World Evaluation
In simulation, tracking accuracy across commanded forces of 5 to 25 N yielded gains of 1.03 to 1.06 with in-contact errors of roughly 1 N. Incorporating force control incurred minimal whole-body tracking degradation: root error increased by only 1.3 to 3.2 cm, and hand position error increased by at most 8.0 mm. On the real standing G1 tested with a handheld force gauge, the controller exerted approximately 91% of the commanded force in steady state with a mean absolute error of about 1.1 N.

### IV-C Task 1: Push Gantry
The robot places both hands on a heavy wheeled gantry carrying a suspended robot and pushes it forward to a target distance. The robot must overcome static friction to initiate movement, and mismatched hand forces cause the gantry to veer off course. Furthermore, the swinging suspended robot introduces dynamic load shifts. FLoRe succeeded in 7/10 trials, whereas the position-only baseline (DP) succeeded in only 2/10. DP frequently veered due to unbalanced hand forces or failed to overcome friction entirely.

### IV-D Task 2: Rotate Box
The robot pinches both edges of a table-top box, rotates it by approximately 50 degrees, and drags it 0.5 m before releasing. This requires balancing dragging friction against internal pinching forces to prevent slipping without crushing the box. FLoRe succeeded in 9/10 trials, compared to 3/10 for DP. DP either stalled against the heavy box or lost balance and fell when pulling aggressively.

### IV-E Task 3: Wipe Board
The robot presses an eraser against a whiteboard to clean along a marked path. Visual inputs alone cannot distinguish light touching from firm contact. To test robustness, the board was perturbed forward or backward by 3 cm. FLoRe succeeded in 8/10 trials, while DP achieved only 3/10. When the board was shifted away, DP hovered in the air without contact; when shifted closer, it pressed excessively and stalled.

### IV-F Ablations and Key Findings
Ablation experiments on force pathways revealed critical insights:
- Removing force command outputs (F-cmd) caused task success to drop sharply from 80% to 36.7% ($p=0.001$). Even with force feedback, position-only commands cannot compensate for contact dynamics.
- Removing force observation inputs (F-in) lowered the success rate to 66.7%. While less catastrophic than omitting force commands, force sensing clearly aids contact detection and disturbance adaptation.

Top (simulation): The robot maintains balance and whole-body trajectories while applying precise target forces to randomized virtual planes. Bottom (real robot): When an operator pulls the robot's hand, it yields compliantly without excessive resistance.

In Rotate Box (bottom left), the baseline falls under the heavy load. In Wipe Board (bottom right), the baseline hovers without maintaining contact force.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Major Step Toward Contact-Capable Humanoids
sections.summary: FLoRe establishes force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation through an integrated design spanning force-annotated demonstrations to compliant whole-body control. It lays a solid foundation for mastering contact-rich everyday skills unattainable by position tracking alone.
sections.details:
FLoRe introduces an accessible pipeline that records motion and contact wrenches simultaneously through handheld human demonstrations, avoiding expensive teleoperation rigs or laborious data collection on real robots.

Crucially, by dynamically shifting target positions using integrated force errors, the hybrid compliance controller exerts precise forces in unknown environments while preserving whole-body balance under external loads—one of the hardest problems in humanoid control.

The dramatic performance gap on three real-robot tasks (80% vs. 26.7%) underscores that contact force must be treated as a first-class citizen in humanoid loco-manipulation. This framework represents a significant milestone toward practical humanoid robots capable of interacting confidently with the physical world.

takeaways: Directly incorporating end-effector contact forces into policy inputs and outputs dramatically improves task success in humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation.

Shifting hand target positions via integrated force errors in the low-level controller enables accurate force tracking under unknown contact stiffness alongside passive compliance on uncommanded axes.
Force-annotated whole-body demonstrations can be collected at scale using handheld force-sensing grippers and affordable body trackers, without requiring teleoperation setups.
Ablations show that generating feedforward force commands from the policy to the controller has a more dominant impact on task success than providing force feedback observations alone.
limitations: A sensor noise floor of 1.25 to 1.50 N prevents the system from reliably commanding or tracking very small contact forces below 1.5 N.
Because simulation training relies on contact planes modeling normal forces, force tracking gains in lateral (shear) and downward directions are slightly lower than along the surface normal.
During heavy whole-body pushing tasks like the gantry, large peak forces coinciding with foot swing phases can occasionally destabilize the robot and cause falls.
